component_records.title: Bid governance, compliance and contract obligations
component_records.description: A single compliance workstream owns every legal, contractual and commercial obligation in the response. It records the Vendor's acknowledgment and acceptance of all RFP terms, exhibits and attachments (R010) and confirms the proposal relies only on the City's terms and conditions, with any exceptions documented rather than substituted (R133). It confirms that all data, materials and documentation originated and prepared for the City belong to the City (R048), that the submittal is not designated proprietary in whole and that the City alone determines what is proprietary (R131), and that the Vendor bears all proposal development costs (R128). It commits the Vendor to notify the City in writing of any known or reasonably knowable RFP error before submission, accepting that a failure to do so is at the Vendor's risk with no later compensation or time relief (R126). It commits to delivering a certification of insurance before any work begins (R134), with an underwriter's endorsement naming additional insureds and a surety admitted in the State of Washington (R135). It also confirms the Vendor will submit questions by the August 28, 2024 3:00 p.m. PT deadline (R004) and will present its functional and technical demo to the City against the pre-defined demo script (R044) after attending the pre-demo logistics meeting (R045).

component_records.title: Programme management, methodology and phased plan
component_records.description: Delivers a defined, proven implementation methodology (R040) expressed as a sample project plan with phases, tasks and timeline, and a phased rollout that the City approves before mobilisation (R012). The plan is anchored to the March 2025 to January 2027 implementation window (R034) and commits all in-scope modules to go live by January 1, 2027 (R042), with phase gates, cutover criteria and a contingency reserve in the schedule. It names City resources by role, responsibility and average time per month and the vendor resources by role, responsibility and average time per month, so the City can see its own staffing commitment. It also carries the process improvement strategy through implementation (R013), using the City's stated intent to adopt vendor best practices rather than replicate Eden, and the business change management methodology and tools used.

component_records.title: Integrated ERP software: Financials and HCM modules
component_records.description: Supplies the integrated ERP suite that satisfies the City's functional and technical requirements (R005) and includes the modules and functionality defined in the Requirements document issued with the RFP (R011). The Financial scope replaces Eden's General Ledger, Purchasing, Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Project and Grant Accounting and Capital Assets (R015), and the HCM scope replaces Eden's Human Resources, Time and Attendance and Payroll as part of the ERP suite (R016). Enterprise Cashiering replaces Quadrant (R017), and the Budget function (R018) and the ACFR function (R019) are delivered inside the suite in place of the City's Excel workbooks. The proposal demonstrates that all modules the City requires are offered (R035) and that the solution meets the functional and technical requirements in depth (R036), with every requirement line item rated on the City's 4/3/2/0/F scale (R115) and the estimated cost of each rating-2 modification stated (R117).

component_records.title: Technology architecture, security and hosting
component_records.description: Delivers the platform, database and accessibility approach that adheres to the City's IT strategy (R037), presented as hosted, on-premises and SaaS architecture options with data centre locations and redundancy, hardware specifications, mobile options, remote access, integration tools and update scheduling. It sets out the security model, SSO/SAML, multi-factor authentication and breach notification, and states the security standards the system meets. It also documents the backup strategy and disaster recovery services covering backup, redundancy and location, distinguishing baseline from premium support levels, and the post go-live tools and services the City receives.

component_records.title: Integration with retained City systems
component_records.description: Delivers the integration layer and demonstrates the integration experience and tools the Vendor offers (R038). Named integrations are built and tested for NeoGov recruiting (R020), Power Time police scheduling and time and attendance (R021), Amanda permitting, planning and land management (R022), MyBuildingPermit.com permitting, planning and land management (R023), RecTrac parks and recreation (R024) and Class for the Dumas Bay Conference Center (R025). The integration review covers OpenGov constituent transparency (R026) and SharePoint document management (R027), with a documented feasibility assessment and recommended approach for each. The design deliberately requires no integration with SeeClick Fix 311 (R030) or Esri GIS (R031), keeping those systems outside the ERP boundary. Where a best-of-breed HCM component is proposed, the integration to the selected ERP is demonstrated and documented (R007).

component_records.title: Enterprise asset and fleet management disposition
component_records.description: Addresses the City's Excel and shadow-system enterprise asset management capability, whose disposition is still under review, by assessing the current spreadsheets and shadow systems, mapping them to the ERP Capital Assets and maintenance functions, and presenting the City with a costed recommendation to absorb, integrate or retain them (R028). It does the same for the Excel and shadow-system fleet management capability, with a documented disposition recommendation and, where the City elects to absorb it, a configured fleet module and conversion plan (R029). Both assessments are delivered as decision papers at the design phase so the City can approve a disposition before build begins.

component_records.title: Data conversion, testing, training and report development
component_records.description: Delivers the data conversion methodology and a recommended conversion scope by module, including years of history and data elements, covering Eden financials, Eden HCM and payroll, Quadrant cashiering and the Excel Budget and ACFR workbooks. It delivers the testing methodology and tools, including conference-room pilots and user acceptance testing, and the training methodology and tools with role-based curricula for the City's named and concurrent users. It delivers the report development approach, including the Budget and ACFR reporting that replaces the City's spreadsheets, and the post go-live support model with support hours, guaranteed response times, escalation paths, baseline versus premium support comparison, and user groups and conferences. All of these services are priced as itemized implementation lines so the City can see the cost of each.

component_records.title: Pricing on Exhibit A with stated assumptions
component_records.description: Completes the Exhibit A Pricing Summary (R068) with pricing that is comprehensive of all taxes and available discounts (R069) and valid for 180 days from the response date (R070). It states the software cost for the user counts defined in the RFP, with one sheet for each deployment option, SaaS and on-premises (R071), and includes all implementation services costs required for go live: software deployment, data conversion, system configuration, report development, testing and training (R072), plus ongoing maintenance for Years 1-10 (R073). It prices the Financials deployment at 130 named and 85 concurrent users (R139) and the HCM deployment at 400 FTEs and 744 W2s (R140), itemizes Year 1 software for the listed Financial modules (R141) and HCM modules (R142), itemizes implementation services across Implementation, Data Conversion, Training, Report Development, Integration, Travel and Other (R143), itemizes subscription and maintenance for each of Years 2 through 10 (R144), and states the assumptions behind each software, implementation and maintenance line (R145).

component_records.title: Vendor credentials, references and demo readiness
component_records.description: Demonstrates the Vendor's organisational strength and viability, including experience with government entities (R039), and evidences successful implementations for cities of similar size and scope (R006). It supplies three current and two prior customer references for the proposed software on the Exhibit B forms, with preference given to Washington State public sector clients, and provides the reference detail the City asks for: customer name, employee count, population, contact name and title, telephone and email, software scope, implementation duration, go-live date and reason for change. It also prepares the demo team to present the product on-site against the pre-defined demo script, covering the City's functional and technical requirements and the application's best practices and adaptability to user preferences.

finding_verdicts.label: R049 <-> R131: All pages or sections of submitted documents that the firm considers proprietary must be clearly labeled as such. / A vendor may not designate its entire submittal as proprietary, and the City alone determines what information may be considered proprietary.

items.text: The City of Federal Way, Washington, issued this RFP on August 16, 2024 for ERP software and implementation services.
Federal Way incorporated in February 1990 and changed from a council-manager to a mayor-council form of government in November 2010.

The City's current core financial and HR systems are Eden (General Ledger, Purchasing, Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Project and Grant Accounting, Capital Assets, Human Resources, Time and Attendance, Payroll), Quadrant for Cashiering, and Excel spreadsheets for Budget and ACFR.

The City retains NeoGov (Recruiting), Power Time (Police scheduling and time), Amanda and MyBuildingPermit.com (permitting, planning, land management), RecTrac (Parks and Recreation), Class (Dumas Bay Conference Center), OpenGov (constituent transparency) and SharePoint (document management), and expects these to integrate with the new ERP.
The City wants process improvement through new systems and intends to adopt the selected Vendor's best practices rather than replicate current practices.
The City's financials are sized at 130 named users and 85 concurrent users, and its Human Capital Management scope at 400 FTEs and 744 W2s.
The City is open to best-of-breed Human Capital Management vendors provided their solution can integrate with the selected ERP system.
The City intends to purchase an integrated ERP solution covering the modules and functionality defined in the Requirements document issued with the RFP.

The solution must replace Eden for General Ledger, Budget, Project and Grant Accounting, Purchasing and Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Capital Assets, Enterprise Cashiering, Human Resources, Time and Attendance and Payroll.
The City expects implementation in a phased approach, or as recommended by the selected Vendor and approved by the City.
Implementation is scheduled to run from March 2025 through January 2027.
The preferred Vendor must have experience successfully implementing the proposed solutions for cities of similar size and scope of services.

Pricing must cover software Year 1, implementation services (implementation, data conversion, training, report development, integration, travel, other), and subscription or maintenance for Years 2 through 10.

The Implementation section must describe methodology with a sample project plan, City and vendor staffing, process improvement strategy, change management, data conversion by module, testing, training and report development.
Proposals are scored on Software 30 points, Implementation 25, Technology 15, Vendor 15 and Cost Value 15.
The Implementation criterion requires Go Live for all modules in scope by January 1, 2027.
Vendor questions are due August 28, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT, answers are posted September 5, 2024, and proposals are due September 17, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT.
Finalists are selected in October 2024, software demos occur in December 2024, due diligence in January 2025, and contract negotiations from January 2025 onward.
Finalists must demo the product on-site against a pre-defined Demo Script, and demos are judged on script adherence and on demonstrating the City's functional and technical requirements.

Every requirement line item must be rated and commented, with ratings of 4 (standard/configuration), 3 (third-party integrated, named), 2 (modification, with estimated cost), 0 (not available) or F (future release with month and year), and applications missing a significant number of required features may be eliminated.
Proposals must include three current and two prior customer references similar in size and scope to the City's project, with preference for Washington State public sector clients.
No contract will be awarded until it is approved by City Council.
Proposals must not exceed 100 pages, excluding a Vendor sample contract, and must be submitted as one electronic PDF plus one completed Requirements document in MS Word format.
Each requirement response is limited to 100 words, and the cover letter is limited to two pages.

Pricing must be submitted on the Exhibit A Pricing Summary, one sheet per deployment option (SaaS or on-premises), comprehensive of all taxes and discounts, and valid for 180 days from the response date.
The ERP Requirements document is provided as a separate Word document that vendors must complete without changing its format, font, numbering or page breaks, and blank responses may cause rejection.

The Technology overview must cover hosted, on-premises and SaaS architecture options, data center locations and redundancy, hardware specifications, mobile options, remote access, integration tools and update scheduling, and the Security overview must cover the security model, SSO/SAML, multi-factor authentication and breach notification.
All proposal information becomes the City's property and public record, no vendor may mark its entire submittal proprietary, and the City makes the sole determination of what is proprietary.
The awarded Vendor must provide certification of insurance before any work begins, with an underwriter's endorsement naming additional insureds and a surety admitted in the State of Washington.
Vendors must document any exceptions to the RFP content and disclose any contract terminated for convenience or non-performance, or legal action with a customer, in the past five years.
The City of Federal Way issued the RFP on August 16, 2024, with vendor questions due August 28, 2024 at 3:00 p.m. PT.
No contract will be awarded until it is approved by City Council.
Implementation is scheduled to run from March 2025 through January 2027, with all modules in scope going live by January 1, 2027.
The City wants process improvement through new systems and intends to adopt the selected Vendor's best practices rather than replicate current practices.

The City's current core financial and HR systems are Eden (General Ledger, Purchasing, Contract Management, Accounts Payable, Accounts Receivable, Project and Grant Accounting, Capital Assets, Human Resources, Time and Attendance, Payroll), Quadrant for Cashiering, and Excel spreadsheets for Budget and ACFR.
The City intends to purchase an integrated ERP solution covering the modules and functionality defined in the Requirements document issued with the RFP.
The City's Technology criterion scores the platform, database and accessibility approach against its IT strategy.
The City retains NeoGov, Power Time, Amanda, MyBuildingPermit.com, RecTrac, Class, OpenGov and SharePoint and expects these to integrate with the new ERP.
The City is open to best-of-breed Human Capital Management vendors provided their solution can integrate with the selected ERP system.
The City's enterprise asset management and fleet management capabilities currently run on Excel and shadow systems, with disposition still under review.
The City's financials are sized at 130 named users and 85 concurrent users, and its Human Capital Management scope at 400 FTEs and 744 W2s.
Pricing must cover software Year 1, implementation services, and subscription or maintenance for Years 2 through 10.
Pricing must be submitted on the Exhibit A Pricing Summary, one sheet per deployment option, comprehensive of all taxes and discounts, and valid for 180 days.
Proposals must include three current and two prior customer references similar in size and scope to the City's project, with preference for Washington State public sector clients.
Finalists must demo the product on-site against a pre-defined Demo Script, judged on script adherence and on demonstrating the City's functional and technical requirements.

The Requirements document issued separately with the RFP is assumed to define the complete module and functionality scope, and the bid prices and rates against that document as the authoritative scope list.
The bid is assumed to be a full ERP bid covering both Financials and HCM, with any best-of-breed HCM component offered only as an integrated option rather than as a standalone partial bid.

Full compliance with the City's functional and technical requirements is assumed to be the target, with any gaps disclosed as rated modifications or future releases rather than as accepted partial compliance.
The bid proposes its own phase structure and sequence, subject to City approval, rather than waiting for the City to prescribe the phasing.
The January 1, 2027 go-live is treated as a firm commitment for all modules in scope, not merely a scored preference.
For the rows marked 'Yes or Part of ERP Suite', the bid delivers the function inside the ERP suite, using interfaces only where the suite has no equivalent.

For OpenGov and SharePoint the bid delivers a documented integration feasibility assessment and recommended approach, and for enterprise asset and fleet management a costed disposition recommendation, rather than committing to a fixed integration build before the City decides.
The 100-page cap is treated as a hard limit applying to the PDF proposal, with the completed Requirements document in Word submitted alongside and not counted toward it.
The 100-word limit is applied per requirement line item only, with narrative sections written to their own stated limits.
Both deployment options priced are SaaS and on-premises, each on its own Exhibit A sheet.
Project and Grant Accounting is priced as a single line item, treating the duplicate listing in the template as a drafting duplication.

Insurance is priced on the assumption of customary public-sector coverages (commercial general liability, auto, workers' compensation, professional/cyber liability and crime) with the City named as additional insured, pending the City's stated limits.

The demo script and pre-demo meeting details are assumed to be issued to finalists with the notification, and the bid team plans a full-day on-site demo prepared from the City's functional and technical requirements in the interim.
The five references are assumed to be customers live on the proposed software, with 'current' meaning under an active subscription or maintenance agreement.
The sample contract documents are assumed to be supplied as part of the response, using the Vendor's standard SaaS licence, maintenance, SLA and statement-of-work templates.
The Requirements document is assumed to be the binding acceptance baseline once incorporated into the contract, with requirements outside it treated as change requests.
The stated question and proposal deadlines are assumed to hold as published, with any City rescheduling communicated by addendum that the bid team incorporates.

Requirements document not in hand, so scope and price are unpriced guesses. The module and functionality scope is defined by a separate Requirements document that the bid team does not yet hold, yet the proposal must rate every line item, price each rating-2 modification and commit to full compliance. If the document contains modules or depth beyond what the bid assumes, the fixed Exhibit A pricing and the January 1, 2027 commitment are built on an incomplete scope and the bidder either under-prices the work or must later claim change orders against a contract that treats the document as the acceptance baseline. The scope list is explicitly deferred to a document outside the RFP text, while pricing, ratings and the go-live date are all mandatory and binding; the bid team cannot validate its cost build without it.

January 1, 2027 go-live treated as firm for every module. The proposed solution commits all Financials, HCM, payroll, cashiering, budget/ACFR and retained-system integrations to a single January 1, 2027 go-live inside a March 2025 to January 2027 window. Payroll and cashiering cutovers, the ACFR reporting build and six named third-party integrations all landing in the same date leaves no float; any slip becomes a missed contractual date rather than a scored preference. The RFP states the date as an evaluation factor and the solution converts it into a firm commitment for all modules, while the RFP does not settle whether it is contractual or whether modules may go live in sequence.

Retained-system integrations are mandatory but their interfaces are undocumented. Six named integrations (NeoGov, Power Time, Amanda, MyBuildingPermit.com, RecTrac, Class) are mandatory, but the RFP gives no interface specifications, data volumes or vendor cooperation commitments for any of them. If a retained vendor does not expose a usable API or charges for access, the integration build expands in scope and cost after the price is fixed. The integrations are mandatory requirements with no technical detail in the RFP, and third-party vendor behaviour is an assumption the bid cannot verify before submission.

Demo script and pre-demo logistics unavailable before finalist notification. Finalists are judged on adherence to a pre-defined demo script that is only issued with the notification, and must attend a pre-demo meeting whose date, time and location the RFP does not give. A demo prepared from the requirements alone may miss scripted scenarios, and a missed or unattended pre-demo meeting risks a low Implementation or Software score at the stage where the shortlist is decided. The script is a referenced document not in the RFP and the pre-demo meeting has no stated logistics, yet both are mandatory and directly scored.

OpenGov, SharePoint, asset and fleet rows left as assessments rather than deliverables. The solution answers the 'Review' rows (OpenGov, SharePoint) and the 'TBD' rows (enterprise asset management, fleet management) with feasibility assessments and costed disposition papers rather than built integrations or configured modules. If the City reads those rows as required deliverables, the proposal is scored as non-compliant or the work arrives later as unpriced scope. The RFP does not say whether these rows require an integration, an assessment or nothing, and the solution resolves the ambiguity in its own favour without City confirmation.

Rating-2 modifications priced before the requirements are known. Every requirement line must be rated on the 4/3/2/0/F scale and each rating-2 modification must carry an estimated cost, with applications missing significant features subject to elimination. With the Requirements document unavailable, modification estimates are guesses; under-estimating them under-prices the build, over-estimating them weakens the Software score. The rating and cost-per-modification obligations are mandatory and scored, and the document that determines how many modifications are needed is not in hand.

Best-of-breed HCM option may not be evaluated against full ERP bids. The RFP is open to best-of-breed HCM vendors, but it does not say whether a partial HCM bid is acceptable or how it is scored against a full ERP bid. The solution assumes a full Financials-plus-HCM bid with best-of-breed only as an integrated option; if the City expected a standalone HCM offer, the bid is priced and shaped for the wrong competition. The RFP leaves the partial-bid question open and the solution resolves it by assumption, which changes both the price and the evaluation basis.

Proprietary-labelling conflict risks disclosure of pricing and design. One requirement lets the firm label proprietary pages while another forbids designating the whole submittal proprietary and reserves the determination to the City, and all proposal information becomes a public record. A bidder that labels aggressively risks a non-responsive finding; one that does not risks its pricing and design being disclosed to competitors. The two requirements conflict directly and the City's standard for confidential treatment is undefined, so either labelling choice carries a cost.

Insurance coverages and limits unstated, so cost and insurability are unknown. The RFP requires a certificate of insurance and an underwriter's endorsement naming additional insureds with a Washington-admitted surety, but states no coverage types, limits or additional-insured parties. The solution prices insurance on an assumed customary public-sector set; if the City's actual limits are higher, the cost is unplanned and the certificate may not be obtainable before work starts. The requirement is mandatory and gating (before any work begins) while the limits that drive the premium are absent from the RFP.

Two deployment options priced in parallel doubles the pricing effort and the risk of inconsistency. The solution prices both SaaS and on-premises on separate Exhibit A sheets, each itemized by module and service line for Year 1 and by year for Years 2-10. Two full cost builds against an incomplete requirements scope, with a 180-day price validity, multiply the chance of an arithmetic or assumption mismatch between sheets and of one option being priced below cost. The RFP requires one sheet per deployment option and the solution commits to both, while the scope document that would make the pricing reliable is not yet available.

City staffing commitments and best-practice adoption are assumed, not agreed. The plan names City resources by role and monthly time commitment and relies on the City adopting vendor best practices rather than replicating Eden. If the City's subject-matter experts are less available than the plan assumes, or if users insist on Eden-equivalent behaviour, configuration and change-management effort grows and the go-live date moves. The RFP states an intent to adopt best practices but does not commit City staffing levels, and the solution's schedule depends on both.

Proposal format and page limits are ambiguous and a deviation can disqualify. The 100-page cap is worded once as a recommendation and once as a hard limit, the required section order is referred to a table not present, and the 100-word limit is stated both generally and per line item. A proposal that misreads the cap or the order can be classified non-responsive, and the Requirements document in Word may or may not count toward the page count. The RFP states the limits inconsistently and makes format deviation a disqualification ground, while the solution resolves each ambiguity by assumption.
